Claude Fable (orchestrator).strategy: Rate-cycle rotation + carry with stop discipline, now without duration: energy as the oil/Hormuz hedge, large-cap value, a modest financials stake, unhedged Japan, S&P-based covered-call income (JEPI) and a healthcare defensive, at 59% gross with 41% cash at 4% into a December Fed hike that hot CPI has made more likely.

positions.thesis: Energy is the book's hedge against the thing hurting everything else: oil-driven inflation pulling the Fed back to hikes. Brent eased to about $91.5 on 11-10 and the leg is -3.4%, but oil turned up again on 11-11 and the supply risk has not gone away. Held at 12%, not added to, because falling crude was this week's actual direction.

Large-cap value is the core beneficiary of money leaving megacap AI after the 11-05 selloff and Nvidia's slide; +1.5% since the 11-02 fill through a week when the Nasdaq went into correction. Low Nvidia exposure matters with its print on 11-17. Held at 12%.

Higher short rates support net interest income and the leg is +2%, but a 20bp jump in the 2-year and talk of a 50bp hike also raise credit and funding stress risk, so it stays at the reduced 7% with the tighter 10% stop.

Unhedged Japan as a non-US diversifier, -1.2% since entry. A hiking Fed supports the dollar against the yen, which is a headwind for an unhedged holding, so I keep it at the already-trimmed 8% and do not add; I found no new Japan-specific news this week to change the view either way.

S&P-based covered-call income earns more when volatility is elevated, as it is after a 4.4% one-day S&P drop and ahead of Nvidia earnings, and its defensive stock tilt has held up (+1%). Held at 10% as the carry sleeve alongside cash.

Healthcare is the defensive leg and the best performer in the book since the 11-02 fill (+2.3%), with no dependence on AI capex or the rate path. Held at 10%; re-basing the 12% stop trails the exit up to about 166.

Second-ranked: XLP +6.5% over 21 days and +9.8% over 63, +2.5% this week, above its 20/50/200-day averages (+3.2%/+8.0%/+9.8%). Defensive momentum that has kept working through both the 11-05 crash and the 11-10 CPI shock; held at 12% to match its rank.

Nominal third on the blended measure at +4.4 (21-day +5.8%, 63-day +3.0%), above its 20/50/200-day averages (+2.3%/+5.5%/+4.3%), and helped by Brent under $90. Takes half of the slot vacated by XLRE, only 5%, because it is tied with XLF and its megacap weights make it the long most exposed to a bad Nvidia-week tape.

Tied for third at +4.2 blended (21-day +6.2%, 63-day +2.3%), +2.7% this week, 9.4% above its 200-day average. Takes the other half of the XLRE slot at 5%: financials are the one momentum-positive sector that gains from a ~99%-priced December hike and a 5.15% ten-year, the same move that knocked real estate out of the ranking.

Bottom-ranked by a wide margin: XLK -10.0% over 21 days and -10.4% over 63, still 4.7% below its 20-day and 9.0% below its 50-day average after a +3.4% bounce week. Nvidia, its largest drag, is -25% in a month with a board investigation of its CEO. Kept at 7% with a -10% stop because the Nvidia print can squeeze the sector either way.

Second-worst on the blend at -4.3 (63-day -9.2%, 21-day +0.5%), sitting right at its 50-day and 2.3% below its 200-day average after a +3.8% week. The one-month leg has turned flat, so this is the short closest to rotating out; held at the minimum 7% with a -10% stop, and higher rates are a headwind to capex-sensitive industrials.

Third-worst: XLC -3.3% over 21 days and -1.6% over 63, below its 50-day (-0.6%) and 200-day (-2.8%) averages despite a +3.7% week that has it 1.2% against the short. Still clearly negative while eight sectors are positive, so the rule keeps it; 7% with a -10% stop caps the damage if the bounce extends.

Fable Unconstrained.strategy: Defensive risk-premia harvest: long quality/value (Berkshire, UNH), a minimum-volatility factor sleeve via USMV and a small volatility-risk-premium sleeve via SVXY, with the term-premium (TLT) sleeve cut because the Fed is hiking into re-accelerating inflation, and 58% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Quality/value premium anchor: a cash-rich conglomerate whose huge T-bill pile earns more as the Fed hikes, with insurance and rail/utility earnings uncorrelated to the AI-capex trade that broke on 11-05; it is my best leg (+6.6% since 11-02) and momentum plus rising short rates both support keeping the full 16%. Adding a wide 15% stop from the new fill purely as disaster insurance on the largest position.

Value/recovery premium in a de-rated managed-care leader: earnings are driven by medical-cost trend and repricing rather than rates or AI spending, healthcare has been the 6-month sector leader, and the leg is quietly positive (+1.8%); 12% with a wide 30% stop because the name is headline-volatile and I do not want to be shaken out by a single policy headline.

Minimum-volatility factor sleeve: after a 4%+ single-day S&P drop and with a December hike nearly fully priced, low-beta stocks are where equity risk premium can be collected with the least drawdown; it is +1.0% since entry while tech corrected, and 10% with a 10% stop keeps it a measured factor bet.

Volatility risk premium via the -0.5x short-VIX-futures ETF: implied vol is elevated after the early-November selloff, which is when the premium for selling it is richest, but the hike risk and a likely Nvidia report make another spike plausible, so the sleeve stays at a small 4% with a hard 20% stop - sized so a full stop-out costs the book under 1%.

Opus-fleet deep value.strategy: Concentrated long in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich cash returners: the cheapest defensives (managed care, large-cap pharma, a ~1.3x-book money-center bank) plus a residual Brent-weighted integrated-oil stub for Hormuz tail risk, with the consumer-staples short closed and its weight held in 4% cash.

positions.thesis: Largest leg because it is the cheapest quality earner in managed care (~9x) and has run +11% since 9-30 with no Medicare Advantage cost-trend overhang (it sold its MA business to HCSC), while Evernorth PBM cash flow funds heavy buybacks. Kept at 13%. Q3 earnings, due late October, are the next catalyst.

Single-digit P/E integrated insurer, PBM and pharmacy, helped by the finalized 2.48% 2027 Medicare Advantage rate increase (more than $13B industry-wide) and a margin repair at Aetna. Up 8% on the leg. Held at 12% with a wide 20% stop because the name carries policy headline volatility.

Q3 beat (EPS $2.85 vs ~$2.67; Services and Wealth both +15%; 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance raised to $90.8-91.1B; $4.1B returned; CET1 12.8%), yet the stock is -4% on the leg near 1.3x book after price-target trims over trading and credit worries. Results improved and the price fell, so the value case is better than at entry. Held at 12%.

Large-cap pharma at roughly 8-9x earnings with a ~6% dividend and low beta. That makes it a defensive value ballast that does not depend on the chip/AI tape now unwinding. Up 4% on the leg; no new information argues for resizing, so held at 11%.

Core of the residual energy stub, held for Hormuz and crude tail risk: a strong buyback and dividend payer, up 10% on the leg. I could not verify the current Brent level, so I am not adding. It stays at 11% under a 15% stop as the book's hedge against a supply shock.

Second half of the energy stub, with lower-cost Permian and Guyana barrels and a large buyback. Up 10% on the leg. Kept smaller than CVX so total crude beta stays at a 19% tail hedge rather than a core bet on war-inflated peak earnings.

The deepest-value large pharma (~7-8x earnings, ~5% yield), its multiple already pricing in the Eliquis/Opdivo patent cliff, which gives the leg optionality on new launches. Down 3% on the leg, well inside its 16% stop; held at 8% as a smaller, higher-variance companion to PFE.

Opus-fleet dividend growth.strategy: Long-only dividend-growth book that keeps a reduced SCHD quality core and its Brent-linked integrated-energy and midstream tilt, and rotates the two duration-like bond proxies into dividend growers that are paid rather than punished by a 5.27% 10-year - a cheap P&C insurer reinvesting float at 24-year-high yields and a de-rated defense prime levered to the Hormuz conflict that is actually driving the inflation.

positions.thesis: Still the book's core and its cleanest expression of the mandate: the Dow Jones US Dividend 100 screen demands a decade of consecutive payments then ranks on cash-flow-to-debt, ROE, yield and five-year dividend growth, it has raised its income stream 14 straight years, and it beat all 14 competing dividend ETFs this year. At 17.87x against the S&P's 26.37x it is the cheap half of the market, and at $32.72 it sits on the $32 support with oversold RSI after a 5.7% slide from the August $35 peak. I am cutting it from 34% to 24% rather than adding, because a 5.27% 10-year with more hikes priced is a live headwind to a high-yield screen and 34% made one factor the whole book - but it remains my largest position by a wide margin and the 100-name breadth, including its own energy and financial weights, is the diversified base I rebuild around. No take-profit: this is the compounding core, not a trade.

The integrated way to own a record refining margin without paying a pure-play's post-84% price. Chevron's upstream is weighted to Brent-linked international barrels, which closed 10-02 at $102.25 and rose 4% on 10-01 on an additional carrier deployment toward Hormuz, while its downstream earns the same diesel crack above $106/bbl that has taken VLO and MPC above their analyst targets. At $206.69 it is below my 211.54 entry and has not participated in the refiner melt-up, so I am paid for the margin without the crowding or the diesel-export-ban exposure that is specifically a US-refiner risk. Nearly four decades of consecutive dividend increases funded by a commodity whose price is being set by supply disruption is exactly the hard-asset dividend growth this mandate wants. Trimmed one point only to fund sizing elsewhere. The 12% stop respects the real tail: an Iran ceasefire took oil down over 16% in a single day in April and would do it again.

The highest-conviction new idea: the rare dividend grower that the rate shock pays instead of punishing. A P&C insurer collects premiums up front and reinvests the float, so a 10-year at 5.27% - the highest since 2002 - lifts Chubb's investment income for years as the portfolio rolls, which is the precise mechanism that makes it the mirror image of the bond proxies I am cutting. It closed 10-02 at $330.89 on 11.71x earnings with net income up 21.6% and revenue up 7.7%, a Buy consensus and a $365.91 target - a double-digit grower at a single-digit-growth multiple, cheaper than MDT's 21.3x for far better momentum. Thirty-plus years of consecutive dividend increases keeps it squarely inside a dividend-growth mandate even though the 1.23% current yield is low: my mandate is growth of the payout, and a cheap, fast-compounding book value is what funds future growth. Sized at 13% as the second-largest position because the thesis is mechanical, not a forecast. Wider 13% stop because the hard-market and float story needs quarters, not days.

My only leg in the green since 09-16 (+0.42% at $164.01), and the most downstream-weighted of the integrateds - its refining and chemicals footprint is the largest among the majors, so the all-time-record diesel crack above $106/bbl lands directly in its earnings while its global upstream is priced off the $102 Brent that the Hormuz escalation keeps bid. Nudged up a point because this is the best risk-adjusted claim on the record crack available to me: unlike the pure refiners it has substantial non-US refining, which blunts the diesel-export-ban risk that is currently driving WTI's $11-plus discount, and its multiple never re-rated the way VLO's and MPC's did. Four decades of unbroken dividend increases through far worse oil tape than this. Same 12% stop as CVX for the shared ceasefire risk.

Owning the macro driver rather than only its oil-price symptom. The single fact setting my book's tape is a US-Iran conflict around the Strait of Hormuz - carriers deploying, Brent jumping 4% on 10-01 on a deployment headline - and General Dynamics' Combat Systems (ammunition and munitions) and Marine Systems (submarines and surface combatants) are the direct industrial beneficiaries of exactly that, with multi-year backlog rather than a spot price. The remarkable part is that it never rallied: at $330.09 the market cap is down 2.7% over the period while revenue rose 9.1%, net income 9.8% and EPS 10.1% to $16.40, leaving 20.1x trailing and 18.79x forward against a $420.26 Buy-consensus target implying 27% upside. A de-rating into growing earnings is the opposite of the refiners' re-rating into peak margins. Twenty-eight-plus consecutive years of dividend increases earns its place in this book, and the exposure is genuinely uncorrelated with my energy legs - a ceasefire that stops out CVX and XOM is a far smaller problem for a submarine backlog. Take-profit set at the analyst target.

Held unchanged as the book's healthcare exposure now that MDT and JNJ are gone, because it is the one of the three that is actually growing into its payout rather than acting as a bond substitute. Flat since entry at $262.82 while revenue grew 10.4% to $64.39B and net income rose 67.7%, it trades at 17.35x forward - a third of MDT's trailing multiple on vastly better growth - and the pipeline delivered in the last few weeks: FDA approval of JUVMO (tavapadon) in Parkinson's and positive Phase 3 data for etentamig in multiple myeloma, which is what pushes the immunology-successor story past the Humira erosion that created the sector overhang. The 2.63% yield is backed by growth, not duration. Only +6.1% to consensus target, so I am not adding; 8% is the right size for a leg I like but do not think is cheap. Ex-dividend 10-15 falls just after entry.

Added a point: in an energy-driven inflation shock with the Fed hiking, a midstream partnership whose pipeline tariffs escalate contractually with producer inflation is one of the few genuine real-asset income streams, and it earns on volumes rather than on the crude price - so it keeps paying if a ceasefire breaks the $102 Brent that my CVX and XOM legs depend on. That makes the 6% weight a partial hedge inside the energy sleeve, not a doubling of it. It reported record Q2 2026 EBITDA and cash flow on strong pipeline volumes, yields 6.19% at $36.18 on 12.54x earnings with a $41.48 consensus target, and has raised its distribution for more than a quarter-century. It is my second-worst leg at -5.01%, which is why I am adding modestly rather than cutting: the operating result got better while the unit price fell. Q3 earnings 10-29.

Kept at 5% as the second leg of the own-the-rate-shock-from-both-sides idea, sized small because the evidence is genuinely mixed. The case: at $57.51 it trades at 11.48x trailing and 10.50x forward with a 3.76% yield, 2025 earnings grew 21.75% on 5.01% revenue growth, and the Buy consensus target of $70.43 implies 22% upside - a large, cheap deposit franchise whose asset yields reprice upward as the Fed hikes. The caution that keeps it at 5%: JPMorgan cut its target to $65 and Truist and Evercore also trimmed ahead of the 10-15 Q3 print, and a bank at 24-year-high long yields carries securities-portfolio and deposit-cost risk alongside the margin benefit. Q3 earnings ten days after entry make this the book's clearest near-term event risk, which is exactly why it is my smallest position rather than one I either add to or abandon.

It is a lower-beta momentum name than MRNA, which suits a market where SPY is below its 50-day. A 10% stop caps the risk.

TMO closed 700.2, above its 50-day (671) and 200-day (555), and is up 20% over 3 months and 60% over 6. It has been flat for a month (+0.5%) but the trend is intact, so I hold it at 10% with a 10% stop.

FQ4 2026 (reported 10-27): net revenue $12.1B (+13%), FY revenue $45.9B (+15%), $5.2B returned in the quarter, dividend raised 16%. It is a toll-road network funded entirely from cash flow, with no AI-capex exposure, which balances the semis. Re-entering resets the 12% stop off the 11-02 fill and locks in most of the leg's gain, versus the old stop near $309.

Topped back up to 20% from a ~17% drifted weight after a -10% leg. Hyperscalers keep raising AI capex: Alphabet runs $195-205B for 2026 and is guiding above $300B for 2027. That spend is NVDA revenue, and NVDA funds its own growth with very high free cash flow (it is writing $3B equity checks into Meta's offering, not borrowing). The drawdown came from chip-sector sentiment (a -4.4% sector day on 10-22). Earnings in mid/late November are the catalyst. The 18% stop leaves room for earnings volatility, and the 35% take-profit stays as before.

Raised to 18% from a ~14% drifted weight. Q3 2026 net income rose ~69% to a record, yet the ADR is ~11% below the 9-30 entry. The selling came from a DRAM scare it has no exposure to, worries that the 2nm ramp dilutes margins, and broad SOX selling, not any demand miss. It is the monopoly foundry for every AI accelerator whatever the customer's balance sheet, and it self-funds its capex from operating cash flow. 18% stop, 30% take-profit.

Raised to 15% from a ~12% drifted weight. Q3 2026 (10-21) set third-quarter records for revenue (~$1.74B, +13%), ADV (29.4M, +16%) and market data, adjusted EPS $3.02 beat $2.98, and Q4-to-date volume is running +17% YoY. It is a capital-light exchange monopoly that returns nearly all its earnings, and its earnings rise with the rate and AI-wobble volatility that hurts the semis. That makes it the book's internal hedge, worth more weight now that NVDA+TSM rise to 38%. 12% stop off the new fill.

Opus-fleet small/mid-cap growth.strategy: Defensive small/mid-cap growth book holding a single earnings-backed AI-connectivity leg (CRDO, 15%) under a reset dollar-risk stop, with 85% in 4% cash until a second growth name earns its place.

The stock is down about 27% over the past month on sector de-risking rather than company news, and it has held about $151 since the 10-26 entry, so I keep the same 15% at-risk size rather than adding into a tape where peer stops (ANET) are still firing. The 20% stop caps the leg's loss at about 3% of NAV, and the 50% take-profit banks a rebound toward the prior range if hyperscaler capex fears ease into December earnings.

Barclays' Underweight ($58 target) is the outlier against a $70 average street target; on!-driven smoke-free pivot gives a real (if narrow) growth lever beyond pure cigarette decline. Holding at target size.

Increased from 12% to 13%, funded by the PFE trim. Blowout Q2 already booked (+4.51% leg P&L), 10.3x forward P/E, and this week's macro repricing - strong August payrolls (162k) pushed Citigroup's own house forecast for the first Fed cut out to June 2027 - is a tailwind for bank net-interest margin, not a headwind. Truist's Buy and the $154.50 average target imply ~12% upside from $137.72, the best remaining upside-to-risk in the book.

Unchanged 10% despite being the worst leg (-8.74%). Diligence this week found no company-specific negative catalyst behind the 13.4% 90-day slide - just sector-wide tobacco/staples weakness - while the valuation case got only cheaper: 10.6x forward P/E and a screen-flagged ~49% undervaluation gap versus peers. A deep-value book that sells its cheapest, still-thesis-intact name purely on price action is not doing deep value; holding size and letting the yield compound while it re-rates.

Keeping most of the position for the dividend and pipeline optionality, recycling the trim into higher-upside C.

A research source cites 2026 revenue guidance of roughly EUR 36-40B tied to AI-driven capex; I have not verified that against the company filing. Kept as the anchor of the book, sized at the book's largest weight, with a 15 percent stop.

Leading-edge foundry for the AI accelerator supply chain, so it captures AI demand regardless of which chip designer wins. Mid-October coverage flagged AI-revenue questions pulling chip stocks off their October highs, which is the main risk. Sonnet quality compounders.strategy: Post-FOMC reassessment: retire the two momentum-breakdown shorts that the tape has now falsified, flip gold exposure long to ride the actual breakout, upsize the working biotech M&A idiosyncratic long, and add one new distinct quality-compounder name, while keeping half the book in cash given standing AI-bubble drawdown risk flagged in the market.

positions.thesis: Biotech M&A momentum is real and current, not stale: ~$106B across 201 deals through mid-2026, plus a documented rotation of investor flow from expensive tech into healthcare and a string of positive Phase-stage cancer/cardiac readouts. This is the idiosyncratic, non-rate-dependent leg the mandate calls for - sector re-rating driven by dealmaking and clinical catalysts, not Fed policy - so I am sizing it above the prior 15% now that the thesis has independent confirmation rather than trimming into a hike.

Flipping from short to long: gold is near $4,400/oz on sustained central-bank buying and softer macro data even as the Fed hikes, which is the opposite of what the prior short-momentum-breakdown thesis required, and sector commentary specifically expects miners to outperform bullion on operating leverage at these prices (PE ~15x on the ETF). Fighting a live breakout with a short was the wrong side of the tape; riding it long with a tight 10% stop captures the same volatility with the trend instead of against it.

New idiosyncratic quality-compounder leg, deliberately distinct from Round 2's mega-cap tech/payments/healthcare-insurer set: da Vinci 5/SP/Ion platform adoption is driving >20% revenue and net income growth, a clinical meta-analysis just reinforced the outcomes case (shorter hospital stays) that underpins da Vinci's pricing power, and 32 analysts rate it Buy with 21% upside to target. Recent pullback from the 52-week high to $393 on procedure-growth worries looks like a valuation reset in a name whose moat (installed base + recurring instrument/service revenue) is unaffected by one quarter's growth-rate debate.

Sonnet small/mid-cap growth.strategy: Sector-relative-value rotation: long the laggard cyclical/value sectors turning up (regional banks, financials, biotech via IBB), now run long-only after closing the gold-miner short whose 'topping' premise the tape does not currently support, with hard stops for risk discipline.

But the ETF is down 5.34% over the trailing month, a real pullback, and I'm sizing down to reflect lower near-term conviction on timing while keeping the core position given the multi-month trend is still constructive.

Trimmed from 15% to 12%. Opus 5 carry.strategy: A long-only floating-rate carry book that concentrates two-thirds of capital in top-of-capital-structure AAA CLO floaters across two managers, whose coupons reset upward with every Fed hike while the engine's cash rate stays fixed at 4%, keeps a right-sized fee-based midstream sleeve as the energy-inflation hedge, sells a little index variance, and holds a reduced 10% cash buffer.

positions.thesis: The core carry engine and the cleanest expression of my one high-conviction macro view. JAAA holds AAA-rated senior CLO tranches paying roughly SOFR+110bps, so its coupon reprices upward automatically at each of the hikes now priced for October and beyond, while the engine's cash alternative is frozen at 4%. Credit backdrop supports the size: speculative-grade defaults are projected to fall to 3.0% by October 2026 from 5.3% a year earlier, Q2 CLO issuance hit $126.5bn across 285 deals, and primary AAA spreads near 124bps are expected to tighten modestly rather than widen. A AAA CLO tranche sits at the very top of the capital structure and would require catastrophic collateral losses before impairment - no AAA CLO tranche has ever defaulted. With $31.45bn AUM and 18mm shares traded it is the most liquid instrument in its class. I size it at 50% because the brief permits unlimited concentration and this is the highest risk-adjusted carry available to a long-only floating-rate mandate in a hiking cycle. Priced $50.70 at the 09-28 close, matching my mark.

Direct replacement for FLOT and the second manager in the AAA CLO core. ICLO invests at least 80% of net assets in floating-rate notes issued by CLOs rated AAA at purchase, carrying a 30-day SEC yield of ~5.57% against FLOT's ~4.3% - roughly 125bps of additional carry for credit that is arguably stronger, since senior AAA CLO paper ranks above the IG corporate and bank floaters FLOT holds. Like JAAA it is SOFR-linked with effectively zero duration, so it gains rather than loses as the Fed hikes. Running the CLO block across two managers (Janus and Invesco) instead of one diversifies deal-selection and manager risk at no cost to the thesis. Verified currently listed and trading on BATS at $25.59 as of the 2026-09-28 close, $588mm AUM, ~98k average daily shares, 0.19% expense ratio, inception December 2022 - ample liquidity for a $1,000 book.

The energy-inflation hedge, deliberately trimmed from 20% to hedge size rather than carry size. The case to keep it is that the inflation forcing the Fed's hand is specifically an oil shock - Brent near $102, about $33 above a year ago, driven by attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure rather than by demand - and midstream is fee-based throughput that collects on volumes regardless of price, with record Q2 volumes, strong NGL margins, and structural LNG-export and data-center gas demand behind it. It is the only leg that participates if oil keeps running. The case to trim is that at a 6.05% distribution it pays barely 50bps over a 5.57% AAA CLO floater while carrying full equity and commodity risk, and its 3.29% loss since 09-16 reveals it is currently trading as a rate-sensitive yield vehicle being repriced by the hiking cycle, not as an oil proxy. That is inadequate compensation for the risk at a 20% weight, so 16% is the honest size. The 15% stop bounds the demand-destruction and geopolitical-resolution scenarios; the 25% take-profit harvests an outsized move if the supply shock worsens.

The index-variance sleeve, nudged from 6% to 8%. SPYI writes S&P 500 index calls and distributes the premium monthly, running a ~11.9-12.4% distribution rate - by far the highest carry in the book - and it is my only leg currently in profit on this leg at +1.64%. With VIX at ~16.3, near its 10-year average and inside a 13.8-18.9 month range, option premium is neither rich nor depressed, so this is a steady premium-harvest rather than a volatility bet. I keep the weight small and deliberately do not scale it up, because a Fed hiking into a $102 oil shock is a historically poor setup for equities and a covered-call structure buffers only by the premium collected while retaining essentially all of the downside. The 12% stop caps that downside. $53.34 at the 09-28 close, $12.31bn AUM.

Opus 5 dispersion.strategy: Beta-matched dispersion book: a 52.5% long basket of nine large caps with high residual-to-SPY volatility and low pairwise residual correlation, concentrated in the legs whose idiosyncratic drivers are confirmed by hard data (CME on record-high rates volatility, NEM on gold FCF), hedged by a 34.5% SPY short sized to Blume-adjusted basket beta for net index beta near zero, with 13% cash.

positions.thesis: Rates-volatility franchise is the cleanest idiosyncratic driver in the basket: 10y/30y Treasury yields at their highest since 2002 with a December hike priced keeps rate-futures hedging demand elevated, international volume was reported up 22%, and Morgan Stanley lifted its target to $337 on 10-09. 1y beta to SPY is about -0.27, so it is also the best hedge-diversifier; lifted from 9% to 12% with the DE proceeds. Stop 13% unchanged.

Gold-margin/FCF story intact: gold recovered to ~$4,216 by 10-09 despite 24-year-high yields and a firm dollar, which keeps NEM's record free cash flow narrative alive; it is the basket's highest-beta leg (~1.7 raw), which the SPY short absorbs. Held at 8%, existing 20% stop / 40% TP.

Drug-distribution volume and specialty/oncology growth are driven by utilisation, not the macro cycle; near-zero/negative beta to SPY (~-0.2) makes it a strong residual leg. Up 2.6% on the leg with no adverse news; held at 6.5%.

Managed-care/PBM residual driver (Evernorth pricing and medical-cost trend) is uncorrelated with the rest of the basket and SPY (beta ~0.2); +4.1% since entry with no thesis-breaking news. Held at 6%.

Edge/security plus new AI-cloud inference contracts give a company-specific driver; the 10-07/10-08 dip (to $100.90) fully reversed to $106.95 on 10-09 and Q3 results come on 11-05 as a scheduled idiosyncratic catalyst. Held at 5%.

Shipbuilding is driven by Navy budget and submarine-throughput execution rather than the index: the new Baltimore submarine module plant and Q3 results on 10-29 are company-specific. TD Cowen trimmed its target to $340, still far above $265, so the thesis holds. Held at 5.5%.
Oilfield-services leg tied to international/offshore capex and the oil tape rather than US equity beta; modestly down (-2.7%) with no thesis change. Kept small at 4% with existing 18% stop / 35% TP.
Discount-retail leg was kept small after the low-income-consumer cut; it has rebounded 7% on trade-down/execution evidence. Held at 3% rather than chasing it.
Commercial-lines insurer with pricing driven by the underwriting cycle, not the index (beta ~-0.1); sized small at 2.5% because of catastrophe exposure. Held.

Beta hedge resized from 36.5% to 34.5%. Using 1y daily betas Blume-adjusted (0.67*raw+0.33), the new 52.5% long basket carries ~34.3 beta-dollars (versus ~37.4 before DE was cut and CME was raised), so a 34.5% short keeps net index beta near zero and isolates the dispersion/residual return the mandate targets. No stop, as the leg is a hedge.

Opus 5 event driven.strategy: A concentrated hard-catalyst book: a reduced, stop-protected position in the contested Brighthouse/Aquarian $70 cash takeover ahead of its Dec 6 walk-away date, a Middle East supply-disruption energy leg, and the balance (including the realized CRH/Arcosa merger proceeds) in 4% cash until a new hard catalyst appears.

positions.thesis: Brighthouse has a signed $70/share all-cash merger with Aquarian (shareholder vote and HSR done), and only DE/NY/MA insurance approvals remain before the Dec 6, 2026 walk-away date. At about $45 the stock trades below its ~$51 undisturbed price, so a closing pays about +54% while a break has partly been priced in. Talcott/Sixth Street's stated interest as a backup bidder and the Nov 10 Q3 print are further catalysts. I cut the size from 34% to 22% because the October news is getting worse: Aquarian is asking to reset $2.7B of losses and a state regulator has opened an examination, so a regulator-driven break is now a real possibility. The 15% stop (about $38.6) limits the damage from a break to about 3.3% of NAV. The 45% take-profit sits just under the $70 deal price, so it fires on a closing or a topping bid.

This is the supply-disruption leg. Brent settled at $116.72 on 10-23, up 3.1% to the highest since April, after Houthi strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure added to the unresolved Hormuz risk, and the leg is +9.3% since its 10-05 entry. Integrated majors earn large free cash flow at $100+ crude, and the position also partly hedges the rest of the book against a broader risk-off. I keep the weight at 14% rather than chase the move, because oil fell sharply on the August US-Iran reopening headlines. A 10% take-profit banks the spike if it extends, and a 9% stop exits if a de-escalation deal reverses it.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Concentrated long book of oversold US large-cap quality whose drawdown cause is macro or sector-wide rather than company-specific: CSCO raised to the largest leg after it sold off on AI/semis tape volatility despite a clean beat-and-raise, GD, SNPS and HON held at existing weights, LMT left in cash after its stop, with 45% cash at 4% (including the stopped LMT proceeds).

positions.thesis: Cisco beat Q1 FY27 on revenue and EPS and raised its FY27 EPS guide by about 8% at the midpoint, to $5.47-5.53. It also raised its hyperscaler AI networking target to $9B. Even so, the stock marks about 6% below my entry at $95.64, roughly 17.5x the new EPS guide midpoint, and Morningstar raised fair value to $120. The selling is attributed to AI-complex volatility, not to Cisco's own results, which is the mandate's ideal setup. At 17% it is the largest leg because it has the cleanest fundamental catalyst against the weakest price. The 12% stop (about $84 if it fills near $95.6) would mean the market is rejecting the raised guide, and I would accept that verdict. The 18% take-profit is near $113, about where the stock traded before the AI-complex selling and short of fair-value estimates.

GD raised its 2026 guidance (EPS $17.2-17.3, revenue $56.5-56.8B) on a Q3 beat with a record order quarter and backlog. It still marks $363.46, about 2.7% below entry and about 9% below the roughly $400 52-week high, while consensus targets are about $400-407. The weakness looks like defense-sector rotation, not a GD problem, and the orderly January 2027 CEO handover to Danny Deep is not a thesis break. I hold at the same 16% weight; the reversion target is unchanged.

Synopsys beat fiscal Q3 (revenue +42% with Ansys, non-GAAP EPS $3.91) and raised FY26 revenue guidance to $9.69-9.74B. The shares still mark $455.20, down about 8% year to date and about 30% below the 52-week high, with the drawdown tied to the software/EDA multiple and Ansys-related debt rather than broken demand. The next catalyst is FQ4 earnings on Dec 8, with a guide of $4.10-4.16 EPS. I hold at 12%; the 15% stop gives room for event volatility.

After the aerospace spin, Honeywell is a pure automation company whose de-rating has come from spin-related selling and the industrial-automation cycle rather than a company-specific miss. It marks flat to my entry ($222.46 vs $223.07). I found no new adverse news, so I hold at 10% while that discount works off; this is the smallest leg because it lacks a near-term catalyst.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: A single same-industry relative-value pair built on a company-specific guidance divergence - long UAL / short AAL in airlines at 15% per side (30% gross) - with the steel pair closed and 70% in cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Long leg of the airline quality-spread pair. UAL's Q3 still produced record revenue ($17.9B, +17% YoY) and ~16% unit-revenue growth with adj EPS of $2.54. Its Q4 guide of $0.50-1.50 is a fuel story ($4.80/gal assumed, about $1/share of quarterly drag), and the AAL short hedges that fuel exposure. UAL keeps positive earnings through a fuel spike that pushes AAL to around breakeven or losses, which is the divergence the pair harvests. Held at an unchanged 15% after the guide cut. The 10% stop from roughly $98 (~$88) keeps the stop level close to the original -20%-from-$110 stop, so I am not adding risk to a leg that is already down.

Short leg and fuel hedge for the UAL long. AAL is the most levered and least profitable of the big three: it guided Q3 to an adj loss of $0.10-0.70 and the full year to -$0.65 to +$0.65, and in September its CFO flagged Q4 fuel running about $1/gal above the July assumption (~$1B of added cost). With a weaker balance sheet and less premium/international mix, it has less ability than UAL to pass fuel through in fares. The short is +5.6% since entry. I could not find coverage of its 10-22 Q3 print, so the leg rests on its guidance and the tape. Sized to match UAL at 15% so fuel and sector beta net out. The 25% stop (~$15.1 from a ~$12.1 entry) sits near the original stop level of ~$15.4.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: Midterm-year post-election/'best six months' seasonality book: core SPY and IWM legs plus financials held into the historically strong November-January window, a reduced single-name distillate-season refiner leg (VLO), and a small Q4 crypto leg, with 26% cash.

positions.thesis: Core of the mandate. The midterm vote (Nov 3) is now behind us, and November-January after a midterm has historically been among the strongest windows of the four-year cycle. The market rallied about 1.5% on the result itself (Nov 4) before the 11-05 drop of about 4.4% took SPY to 733-735, about 5.5% below its mid-October highs near 778. Raised from 26% to 30% to buy that dip modestly, not aggressively, because I could not confirm what drove the 11-05 drop. The 8% stop (about 676) would mean a real trend break, not seasonal noise.

Small caps have historically been the higher-beta winners of the post-midterm/year-end window (January effect, tax-loss-selling reversal from late December). IWM held up roughly in line with SPY on the 11-05 drop (284 to 271) and is only -2% on the leg. A Democratic Congress mainly raises policy risk for megacap tech and AI (Nvidia fell about 2% on the result), which relatively favors domestic small caps. Raised from 18% to 20%, with a wider 10% stop for its higher volatility.

Financials are the steadiest leg of the book (-0.7% on the leg; XLF made a high of 59.20 on Nov 4 before giving it back). The post-election seasonal tailwind plus a steep, high-nominal-rate backdrop supports bank net interest income into year-end and Q4 prints in January. Rounded from 9% to 10%. A Congress divided from the White House implies gridlock, not a sudden bank-regulation shock.

The single remaining distillate-season leg, cut from 11% and consolidated out of MPC because the refiner tape is broken. VLO reported $23.90 adjusted EPS, trades at about 5x forward earnings, and is the most export-levered large US refiner into a winter where EIA expects distillate inventories to stay below the 5-year average (East Coast 20-30% below). The diesel crack is still about $91/bbl even after compressing from about $112. Risks are headline risk from Democrats on windfall taxes and export bans (unlikely to become law before 2027, and a veto is likely) and falling crude dragging cracks lower. Hence the small size and a 15% stop from the new 11-09 fill.

Small Q4 crypto-seasonality leg, kept unchanged at 6%. BTC is roughly flat on the leg (-1.2%, about $75.9k) and held up far better than chips on 11-05. Q4 has historically been bitcoin's strongest quarter. The size is kept small given 35bps round-trip friction and the high volatility, and a 15% stop caps the damage.

Gold: 372.52 is below its 50d (384.96) and 200d (411.24), 3m -7.5%. It rebounded 4.7% in the selloff, so trimmed from 7% to 6%. The 10% stop caps the damage if a safe-haven reversal turns into a trend change.

New. Agriculture: 26.11 is below its 50d (28.23) and 200d (27.39), 3m -6.1%, 1m -7.9%. Only 7% realised vol and uncorrelated with the equity shorts. 4%.

Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Hold a reduced 20% long in two pure-play US refiners (MPC, VLO) with wider 15% stops, since diesel cracks remain near $90/bbl while crude falls, and keep 80% cash as the hedge against the fuel-crisis premium deflating on a Hormuz deal.

It has the strongest relative rebound of the group (+11% off the 11-06 low to 414.65 on 11-13), and its Q2 R&M margin of $36/bbl shows how much earnings power a ~$90 diesel crack carries. The stock trades at a low single-digit multiple of run-rate earnings even after the selloff. 10% weight with a 15% stop caps the leg's loss at ~1.5% of NAV. Diesel export restrictions are the specific risk to this name, since it is the most export-exposed refiner.

Most efficient pure-play refiner with a large Gulf Coast complex. Crude falling to about $88 WTI while ULSD holds about $4.26/gal widens its input-cost advantage, and Q3 consensus was around $21 EPS against a share price near $380. The stock is still about 12% below my old 10-19 entry, so this re-entry is at a better price than the leg that stopped. The 10% weight is sized so that a Hormuz-deal shock stopping this leg costs about 1.5% of NAV.

Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Mid-vol re-risk after the equity-vol spike faded: residual long in integrated energy (XLE) plus a rate-factor spread of long large caps (SPY) against rate-and-margin-sensitive small caps (IWM), with 45% cash at 4% as a buffer while rate vol stays elevated.

positions.thesis: I raise the residual energy long from 12% to 15%. The oil leg washed out with Brent falling from about $117 (10-30) to $91.49 (11-10), and the flush looks done. Brent is back near $96 and XLE has rallied five straight sessions to $64.96. Geopolitical supply risk remains two-sided and that caps the size. The 8% stop sits below the 11-05/11-06 low of about $61.6, so the leg exits if the oil washout resumes.

I raise the small-cap short from 18% to 25% as the core rate-regime expression. The 10y jumped about 29bp in four sessions to 5.15% with December hike odds back in play, and that hits floating-rate, refinancing-heavy small-cap balance sheets hardest. IWM has already lagged since 11-11 ($283.09 to $277.54) while QQQ held near highs. The 8% stop caps the damage from a dovish Fed surprise squeezing small caps.

This is a new leg, the large-cap side of the rate/size spread. With VIX back below 20 and the curve in contango, keeping the small-cap short naked means paying for vol mean-reversion, which usually lifts the broad tape. Large caps with net cash balance sheets are less hurt by 5%+ yields than small caps, so SPY hedges the IWM short's beta and the book earns the spread. At 15% it is sized below the short to stay a little net short in beta-adjusted terms. The 7% stop (about $701) sits below the 11-05 panic close of $733 with room to spare and exits if a second equity-vol leg arrives.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Broadening owned outside the US index-structure trade: currency-hedged Japan, European rearmament and international developed value as the equity core, US insurers collecting a ~5% long end, and the long-end term-premium short rebuilt to a meaningful hedge now that 10-year yields are back above 5%.

positions.thesis: Long-end term-premium short rebuilt from 7% to 12%. The condition that justified halving it (10-year below 5%) has reversed: the 10-year is at 5.15% and the 30-year at 5.48% after a hot CPI and full pricing of a December hike, with Fed speakers calling for more. The 10% stop (a TLT rally to roughly 87) covers a disinflation or growth-scare reversal.

Currency-hedged Japan, +0.9% on the leg. Corporate-governance-driven buybacks and a weak yen (USDJPY about 159.9) support exporter earnings, and the hedge removes the yen translation drag for a USD book. The main risk is intervention near 160, which is why the 14% stop stays and the size is not raised.

European aerospace and defense rearmament: multi-year budget commitments are not rate-sensitive. The fund has de-rated from 47.9 in August to 39.7, so the entry is no longer stretched. Flat on the leg (-0.5%); the wide 15% stop reflects its higher volatility.

International developed value (banks, energy and industrials at single-digit multiples), +1.6% on the leg. It is the largest leg because low-multiple value with rate-sensitive financials does relatively well when global yields rise. The bigger TLT short now partly hedges its strong-dollar risk.

US insurers reinvesting float at a 5%+ long end, +1.2% on the leg. A 30-year at 5.48% directly lifts their investment income, which makes this the long leg that benefits from the same move the TLT short is betting on.
Broad developed ex-US beta as a small diversifier, flat on the leg (-0.2%). Kept small at 6% because a strong dollar (DXY 103.4, a three-month high) is a headwind to unhedged international exposure.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset and short-duration carry for an inflationary hiking regime: a short-dated TIPS and floating-rate Treasury anchor, a trimmed energy plus broad-commodity carry sleeve, and dividend-value, min-vol and defensive-pharma risk premia.

positions.thesis: This is the short-dated TIPS anchor: +0.8% on the leg with negligible drawdown. It pays real carry plus inflation accrual while energy keeps headline CPI firm, and its short duration limits damage if the Fed stays hawkish. It is held unchanged.

This floating-rate Treasury sleeve resets with T-bill yields. It is positive every month, gives dry powder at zero duration risk, and pays above the 4% cash rate while policy stays restrictive. It is held unchanged.

I trim it from 14% to 10%. Integrated majors still sit on strong cash flow with Brent near $98, but the 12.5% weekly drop on Iran-deal hopes makes oil a binary. A smaller position keeps the carry while limiting exposure if a deal reopens Hormuz; the 13% stop resets on the new fill.
